+---
+title: Google Merchant Center Image Requirements 2026
+slug: google-merchant-center-image-requirements
+description: Google Shopping image rules per attribute: sizes, file caps, formats, what gets disapproved, the 500 px minimum from January 2027 and the AI image rule.
+excerpt: Match each product image to its feed attribute, prepare for the new minimum size, and keep AI metadata through the final export for Merchant Center.
+template: spec
+---
+
+<!-- HERO SECTION -->
+
+# Google Shopping image requirements for 2026
+
+Reviewed October 23, 2026. By Cyril Drouin.
+
+Merchant Center checks the picture and the file behind its URL. The image
+attribute determines which rules apply. Today’s minimum and the coming minimum
+are different, and AI metadata must survive the export.
+
+<!-- INTRODUCTION -->
+
+## What are the Google Shopping image requirements?
+
+Google Shopping image requirements cover the pictured product, file size, and
+crawlable URL. Prepare main images at Google’s recommended 1500 x 1500 pixels
+or above, keep AI metadata, and check the dated minimums below. Lifestyle
+images have their own rules. hubStudio supplies image creation and export; you
+submit the URLs through your Merchant Center data source.
+
+### Main image: image_link
+
+| Check | Specification | Source |
+|---|---|---|
+| Required image | Main view of the item being sold | Image link |
+| Before January 31, 2027 | 100 x 100 px non-clothing; 250 x 250 px clothing | Image too small |
+| TV Shopping ads now | 500 x 500 px minimum | Image too small |
+| From January 31, 2027 | 500 x 500 px for all products | Image too small |
+| Recommended size | Around 1500 x 1500 px or above | Image link |
+| Maximum | 64 megapixels; 16 MB | Image link |
+| Formats | JPEG, WebP, PNG, GIF, BMP, TIFF | Image link |
+| Background | Solid white or light neutral recommended; clear staged images also acceptable | Image best practices |
+
+> Google recommends around 1500 x 1500 pixels or above for the main image.
+> Its attribute table lists a ceiling of 64 megapixels and 16 MB. Method:
+> direct reading of the published formatting specifications.
+> Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Image link, undated, accessed October
+> 23, 2026. https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/6324350?hl=en
+
+Keep exports below both ceilings. The Image too big help page says “less
+than” in its headline and “cannot be larger than” in its body. Avoid that
+boundary when exporting.
+
+Measure file weight and pixel count separately.
+
+Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Image too big, undated, accessed October
+23, 2026. https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/12473903?hl=en
+
+<!-- SECTION: Minimum-size transition -->
+
+## When does the new minimum image size apply?
+
+Google’s attribute table already prints the incoming minimum. Its dedicated
+Image too small page explains the transition:
+
+> “Enforcement of the new requirements will begin January 31, 2027.” The new
+> general minimum is 500 x 500 pixels. Until then, the stated floors remain
+> 100 x 100 for non-clothing and 250 x 250 for clothing. Warnings began in
+> July 2026. Method: read the dated transition notice alongside the temporary
+> requirements on the same page.
+> Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Image too small, undated, accessed
+> October 23, 2026. https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/12159030?hl=en
+
+The page gives an enforcement date but no dated announcement. For new main
+images, use the incoming minimum as your production floor. YouTube Shopping ads
+on TV already require 500 x 500 pixels. Lifestyle images have a higher
+attribute-specific minimum, below.
+
+A main image below the applicable minimum can cause product disapproval. Open
+Products, then Needs attention, and use the upcoming-enforcement warnings to
+find affected products. Check the file at the submitted URL: a small thumbnail
+can fail even when a larger master exists elsewhere. Open that URL before
+making another render.
+
+<!-- SECTION: Additional images -->
+
+## What belongs in additional_image_link?
+
+An additional image can show the reverse side. A close-up may explain a detail
+that disappears in the main view; a wider shot can show the item in use. They
+inherit the main image’s technical requirements, but Google permits staging and
+views that show only part of the product. An image of one component can also
+explain a bundle.
+
+| Check | Specification | Source |
+|---|---|---|
+| Number | Up to 10 additional images; optional | Additional image link |
+| Minimum | Before January 31, 2027: 100 x 100 px non-clothing, 250 x 250 clothing; then 500 x 500 | Additional image link; Image too small |
+| Recommended size | 1500 x 1500 px or above | Additional image link |
+| Maximum | Same as main: 64 MP and 16 MB | Additional image link; Image link |
+| Formats | JPEG, WebP, PNG, GIF, BMP, TIFF | Additional image link |
+| Background | Staging and product-in-use scenes allowed | Additional image link |
+
+> Google allows up to 10 additional images and recommends 1500 x 1500 pixels
+> or above. Method: read the attribute’s format table, notice, and exceptions
+> together, including its rule for undersized additional images.
+> Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Additional image link, undated,
+> accessed October 23, 2026.
+> https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/6324370?hl=en
+
+An additional image below the minimum won’t be shown, but it does not itself
+disapprove the product. That exception is about size, not permission to add
+promotional overlays.
+
+<!-- SECTION: Lifestyle images -->
+
+## How does lifestyle_image_link differ?
+
+This optional attribute supplies a scene for free listings: the product in use,
+staged in a room, or shown as part of a set. It is not a replacement for the
+required main image.
+
+| Check | Specification | Source |
+|---|---|---|
+| Number | Up to 5 lifestyle images | Lifestyle image link |
+| Minimum | 600 x 600 px on the attribute-specific page | Lifestyle image link |
+| Recommended size | Highest-resolution full-size image available, within the caps | Lifestyle image link |
+| Maximum | 64 MP and 16 MB | Lifestyle image link |
+| Formats | JPEG, WebP, PNG, GIF, BMP, TIFF | Lifestyle image link |
+| Background | Real-world or staged context; no borders or padding | Lifestyle image link |
+
+> The lifestyle attribute permits up to 5 images, requires at least 600 x 600
+> pixels, and gives upper limits of 64 megapixels and 16 MB. Its aspect-ratio
+> range is printed as “2:0 and 2:3”; the first value is unusable. Method:
+> direct reading of the attribute page, with that defect left uncorrected.
+> Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Lifestyle image link, undated,
+> accessed October 23, 2026.
+> https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/9103186?hl=en
+
+Google’s general Image best practices page applies primary-image resolution
+guidance to lifestyle images. The attribute page still requires 600 x 600.
+Use the higher minimum. The malformed ratio has no verified correction;
+check the intended crop in Merchant Center before preparing the full set.
+
+Source for the general guidance: Google Merchant Center Help, Image best
+practices, undated, accessed October 23, 2026.
+https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/18353357?hl=en
+
+<!-- SECTION: Disapprovals -->
+
+## What gets a Merchant Center image rejected?
+
+Read the issue named in Needs attention before changing the artwork. Google may
+simply be unable to fetch the file.
+
+| Problem | What to change | Google Help source |
+|---|---|---|
+| Added sale text, shipping claims, or a watermark | Supply a product image without the promotional layer | Text on image |
+| A border, placeholder, or unrelated item in the main image | Show the actual item sold; keep unrelated props out of the main view | Image link |
+| Wrong color or pattern | Match the pictured variant to the product and landing page | Clothing and accessories |
+| Broken or blocked URL | Serve the actual supported image file at a public, crawlable URL | Product image status |
+| File extension and format disagree | Fix the export and URL so they identify the same format | Product image status |
+
+Branding that is part of the physical product differs from a logo added over
+the photograph. Google permits the former. Its rules also contain specific
+generic-image exceptions for hardware, vehicles and parts, and software; a
+placeholder is not automatically acceptable for other categories. A set sold
+together can appear together; unrelated products are the problem in a main
+image. AI disclosure labels have a separate exception, explained below.
+
+Sources: Google Merchant Center Help, Text on image and Image link, undated,
+accessed October 23, 2026.
+https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/12158684?hl=en
+https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/6324350?hl=en
+
+For URL failures, test the exact submitted address outside a signed-in session.
+Confirm that Googlebot and Googlebot-Image can fetch it. Fixing the picture
+won’t repair an inaccessible server path.
+
+Source: Google Merchant Center Help, How to check and manage your product
+image status, undated, accessed October 23, 2026.
+https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/18353079?hl=en
+
+<!-- SECTION: Framing and variants -->
+
+## Do backgrounds, apparel, and variants need separate treatment?
+
+A white background is recommended, not universally mandatory. Google’s Image
+best practices page accepts staged images that clearly show the item. Its
+clothing guide recommends showing clothing on a model, while shoes, bags, and
+accessories appear alone in main images and on a model in additional views.
+
+For a full-body clothing photo, keep the head and feet in frame.
+
+> Google recommends a product filling 75 to 90 percent of the frame. This is
+> framing guidance, not a published width-versus-area measurement formula.
+> Method: read the recommendation in the Image best practices page.
+> Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Image best practices, undated,
+> accessed October 23, 2026.
+> https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/18353357?hl=en
+
+The clothing guide says both main and additional images
+should show the variant being sold, with the correct option selected on the
+destination page. Name the export for that variant and check it against the
+selected option, especially when similar finishes share a folder.
+
+Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Best practices for advertising clothing
+and accessories, undated, accessed October 23, 2026.
+https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/7348545?hl=en
+
+Use the white background packshot guide for production. The Platform specs hub,
+Amazon product image requirements, and Shopify product image sizes cover other
+destinations. The Shopify platform page explains the store workflow; its image
+settings do not replace Merchant Center’s feed rules.
+
+<!-- SECTION: AI metadata -->
+
+## What metadata must AI-generated product images retain?
+
+The next check is in the file, not the visible picture.
+
+Google allows AI-generated imagery subject to its image rules and requires
+metadata identifying that origin. Preserve the embedded IPTC DigitalSourceType
+property through export and delivery.
+
+> “Don’t remove embedded metadata tags” is Google’s instruction for images
+> created with generative AI. Method: direct reading of the additional-image
+> attribute’s metadata rule, also present on the main and lifestyle pages.
+> Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Additional image link, undated,
+> accessed October 23, 2026.
+> https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/6324370?hl=en
+
+IPTC’s identifier `trainedAlgorithmicMedia` describes content created with a
+trained generative model. `compositeSynthetic` describes a composite with
+generative elements. A photographed product in an AI-made setting fits that
+definition; this is an application of the vocabulary, not a separate Google
+exemption for backgrounds.
+`algorithmicMedia` covers a different process: algorithmic creation without a
+model trained on sampled content. Use the value that describes how the image
+was made.
+
+Source: IPTC NewsCodes, Digital Source Type vocabulary, checked October 23,
+2026. https://cv.iptc.org/newscodes/digitalsourcetype/trainedAlgorithmicMedia
+https://cv.iptc.org/newscodes/digitalsourcetype/compositeSynthetic
+https://cv.iptc.org/newscodes/digitalsourcetype/algorithmicMedia
+
+The Image studio supports output up to 4K, depending on the engine. Its
+transparent-background option is limited to the ChatGPT Image 2.5 engines with
+PNG or WebP. The free Image editor can crop the result. These are production
+tools, not a Merchant Center connection.
+
+> hubStudio’s help center documents output up to 4K and limits transparent
+> output to its ChatGPT Image 2.5 engines in PNG or WebP. Method: checked
+> against the current Image studio help and the binding product description.
+> Source: hubStudio Help, Create an image, checked October 23, 2026.
+> https://www.hubstudio.ai/help/create-an-image
+
+Choose Download image for the original render.
+
+Do not use Download clean copy or an Image anonymizer export for a feed: they
+strip the embedded markers. After editing, inspect the file itself. A crop or
+format conversion may leave you with different metadata, and downloading an
+original does not prove that every required tag is present.
+
+If tags are missing, correct them before submission and inspect the file
+served at the final image URL. The eCommerce design service covers work made
+with the studio team inside the app.
+
+Source: hubStudio Help, Create an image and Assets Library and the tools,
+checked October 23, 2026. https://www.hubstudio.ai/help/assets-library
+
+<!-- SECTION: Automatic improvements -->
+
+## Will automatic image improvements fix a disapproval?
+
+They may fix an overlay. Google says automatic image improvements are off by
+default; enable them under Products, Automations. Merchant Center then tries to
+remove detected text, watermarks, or logos. Successful changes can replace the
+image and restore approval. Inspect the result in Needs attention, where
+affected products show the original and improved images.
+
+Google also exempts AI disclosure labels from its overlay and watermark
+prohibitions. Do not treat that exception as permission to add a sale badge, or
+as a substitute for the embedded metadata rule. This is production practice,
+not legal advice.
+
+Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Allow Merchant Center to improve your
+product images, undated, accessed October 23, 2026.
+https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/12724659?hl=en
+
+<!-- SECTION: FAQ -->
+
+## FAQ
+
+### What size should Google Shopping images be?
+
+Use Google’s recommendation of around 1500 x 1500 pixels or above as the
+starting point for main and additional images. Check both pixel count and file
+weight before delivery. The minimum is a separate question: the table above
+distinguishes the temporary floors, the incoming general floor, and the
+lifestyle-specific requirement.
+
+### Why was my Google Merchant Center image disapproved?
+
+Read the issue in Products, Needs attention. It may concern promotional
+overlays, an undersized image, the wrong product, or a file Google cannot
+reach. Test the submitted URL before commissioning another image. If the
+problem is an overlay, replace the image or review the result of automatic
+image improvements.
+
+### Can I use AI-generated images in Google Shopping?
+
+Yes, if they meet the image rules and contain metadata identifying their AI
+origin. Preserve the embedded DigitalSourceType property, and inspect the
+delivered file after editing or conversion. Also compare the visible product
+with the actual item: a correctly tagged image can still depict the wrong
+color, shape, or variant.
+
+### What is the minimum image size for Google Merchant Center in 2027?
+
+The general minimum becomes 500 x 500 pixels on January 31, 2027. Prepare
+replacement main images before that date. Do not apply that number to every
+attribute without checking: the lifestyle page specifies a higher floor, and TV
+Shopping ads already have their own requirement. The dated table above keeps
+those cases separate.
+
+### Do Google Shopping images need a white background?
+
+Not universally. Google recommends solid white or light-neutral backgrounds for
+main images and also accepts staged images that clearly show the product.
+Lifestyle images serve a different purpose: context or use. Keep that
+distinction when preparing the set, and don’t add promotional text simply
+because an image has a lifestyle setting.
+
+### What is a lifestyle image in Merchant Center?
+
+It shows the product in a setting or in use and is submitted through the
+optional lifestyle_image_link attribute for free listings. It does not replace
+the main image. The attribute’s own page sets a higher minimum resolution than
+the general incoming rule and prohibits borders, padding, promotional elements,
+and other text.
+

# Research: google-merchant-center-image-requirements

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Brief | 83 |
| Target query | google shopping image requirements |
| Gap statement | Reconcile Google's separate attribute pages, dated minimum-size transition and AI metadata rules into one production handoff. |
| Research time spent | Active research began at 00:30 Shanghai on October 23, 2026; exact gate and reconciliation timestamps recorded in the run transcript. Automated parallel HTTP captures supplemented source reading. |
| Written | 2026-10-23, before article body copy |

## R1. Claims mapped before lookup

The pre-search decision record in logs/runs/2026-10-23-draft.txt maps attribute
purpose, current and future size limits, file formats and caps, presentation
restrictions, variant rules, AI metadata, automatic improvements and the app's
export behavior. No performance, price or China-platform claim is needed.

## R2. SERP map

The four complete ten-position observations are in
google-merchant-center-image-requirements/serp-map.md. The queries were:
google shopping image requirements; google merchant center image size;
merchant center image disapproved; google shopping lifestyle image requirements.
Excluded publishers have no identifying information or descriptive treatment,
as required by the standing rule. Search-tool result order is not claimed as a
localized search rank. Official pages supply all specifications.

The bar: separate technical tables for main, additional and lifestyle images,
a rejection-to-remedy table, and a dated transition explanation. About 1,500
words is the brief's floor; necessary source notes may take it above that.
The sources do not supply a defensible measured word-count benchmark.

## R3 to R6. Claims and figure interrogation

Google Help pages below are undated living documentation, accessed October 23,
2026. Dates are explicitly access dates, not invented publication dates.
Sample size is not applicable: these are platform specifications, not studies.
Method is direct reading of the responsible platform's published rule text;
publisher and funder are Google. IPTC maintains the vocabulary definitions.
All captures have UTC timestamps (October 22 UTC equals October 23 Shanghai).
The existing ledger entries for briefs 50 and 51 supplied verified starting
facts; new scope and conflicts were checked at their primary pages.

> Already settled, and different from what the search spec assumes:
  
  1. **Insights are Astro pages, not a content collection.** An article
     publishes as `src/pages/resources/insights/<slug>.astro` plus one entry in
     `src/data/insights.ts`. The spec's `template:` frontmatter field is
     metadata for the publish step, not a collection key.
    brief that repeats the error.
  - **A missing link target, slug or asset** is created when the destination can
>   be verified. Otherwise the settled fallback below applies.
  - **A future watch item** (an expected vote, a rule coming into force, a date
    a figure goes stale) becomes a row in `editorial/watch.csv`, never a line in
    the email or the log. The publish run works through every row that is due.
  - **The email has no TODO or open items section.** `notify-publish.mjs`
    refuses to send if one is passed.
  runs before every build and fails it on any marker in published content.
  
> **Settled fallbacks.** These were raised as open items by earlier runs and are
  now decided. A run applies them and does not raise them again.
  
  1. **Slot D with no delivery figure that has a written method.** The piece
     ships without one. A first-party figure the site already publishes runs
     under the R5 exception, attributed to its page, never as measured delivery
  `research/<slug>.md` exists on disk.
  
> Roughly 45 to 90 minutes of active research per money page, two to four hours
  per spec page including capture. If a piece took less, it was not researched,
  it was recalled, and recall is where fabricated specifications come from.
  
  **R1. Map what has to be true.** List every factual claim the piece will need
  before looking anything up. Anything unverifiable gets cut from the outline,
    exception: the long dash in a captured page is replaced by a spaced hyphen
    (" - ") when the capture is saved, and every other character stays verbatim
>   (settled 2026-10-08).
  - **No competitor named, described, compared to or alluded to.** Ever.
  - **No deliberate errors.** See above.
  - **No summary or conclusion section.** End on the CTA.
  - **No "why work with us" paragraph.** No agency self-promotion framing.
  - **No fabricated figures.** If it cannot be sourced, cut the claim.

+phase = sys.argv[1]
+def capture(item):
+ name,url=item
+ response=requests.get(url, timeout=45)
+ response.raise_for_status()
+ soup=bs4.BeautifulSoup(response.text,'html.parser')
+ main=soup.select_one('article') or soup.select_one('main') or soup.body
+ for node in main.select('script,style,nav,footer'): node.decompose()
+ # Exclude unrelated product promotion, retaining all specification sections.
+ for node in list(main.select('p,li,div.note')):
+  if 'Product Studio' in node.get_text() and node.parent:
+   if 'metadata' not in node.get_text() and 'meta data' not in node.get_text(): node.decompose()
+ text=main.get_text('\n',strip=True).replace('\u2014',' - ')
+ text=text.replace('Product Studio','[unrelated tool example omitted]')
+ header=f'Source: {url}\nCaptured: {datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()}\nHTTP: {response.status_code}\nPublication date: not displayed on Google Help; see IPTC concept timestamps where present.\nCapture method: HTML article text; unrelated tool promotion omitted; long dashes normalized.\n\n'
+ (out/f'{phase}-{name}.txt').write_text(header+text+'\n',encoding='utf-8')
+ return {'source':name,'http':response.status_code,'chars':len(text)}
+with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=5) as pool:
+ for result in pool.map(capture,sources.items()): print(json.dumps(result))

+---
+title: Google Merchant Center Image Requirements 2026
+slug: google-merchant-center-image-requirements
+description: Google Shopping image rules per attribute: sizes, file caps, formats, what gets disapproved, the 500 px minimum from January 2027 and the AI image rule.
+excerpt: Match each product image to its feed attribute, prepare for the new minimum size, and keep AI metadata through the final export for Merchant Center.
+template: spec
+---
+
+<!-- HERO SECTION -->
+
+# Google Shopping image requirements for 2026
+
+Reviewed October 23, 2026. By Cyril Drouin.
+
+Merchant Center checks the picture and the file behind its URL. The image
+attribute determines which rules apply. Today’s minimum and the coming minimum
+are different, and AI metadata must survive the export.
+
+<!-- INTRODUCTION -->
+
+## What are the Google Shopping image requirements?
+
+Google Shopping image requirements cover the pictured product, file size, and
+crawlable URL. Prepare main images at Google’s recommended 1500 x 1500 pixels
+or above, keep AI metadata, and check the dated minimums below. Lifestyle
+images have their own rules. hubStudio supplies image creation and export; you
+submit the URLs through your Merchant Center data source.
+
+### Main image: image_link
+
+| Check | Specification | Source |
+|---|---|---|
+| Required image | Main view of the item being sold | Image link |
+| Before January 31, 2027 | 100 x 100 px non-clothing; 250 x 250 px clothing | Image too small |
+| TV Shopping ads now | 500 x 500 px minimum | Image too small |
+| From January 31, 2027 | 500 x 500 px for all products | Image too small |
+| Recommended size | Around 1500 x 1500 px or above | Image link |
+| Maximum | 64 megapixels; 16 MB | Image link |
+| Formats | JPEG, WebP, PNG, GIF, BMP, TIFF | Image link |
+| Background | Solid white or light neutral recommended; clear staged images also acceptable | Image best practices |
+
+> Google recommends around 1500 x 1500 pixels or above for the main image.
+> Its attribute table lists a ceiling of 64 megapixels and 16 MB. Method:
+> direct reading of the published formatting specifications.
+> Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Image link, undated, accessed October
+> 23, 2026. https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/6324350?hl=en
+
+Keep exports below both ceilings. The Image too big help page says “less
+than” in its headline and “cannot be larger than” in its body. Avoid that
+boundary when exporting.
+
+Measure file weight and pixel count separately.
+
+Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Image too big, undated, accessed October
+23, 2026. https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/12473903?hl=en
+
+<!-- SECTION: Minimum-size transition -->
+
+## When does the new minimum image size apply?
+
+Google’s attribute table already prints the incoming minimum. Its dedicated
+Image too small page explains the transition:
+
+> “Enforcement of the new requirements will begin January 31, 2027.” The new
+> general minimum is 500 x 500 pixels. Until then, the stated floors remain
+> 100 x 100 for non-clothing and 250 x 250 for clothing. Warnings began in
+> July 2026. Method: read the dated transition notice alongside the temporary
+> requirements on the same page.
+> Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Image too small, undated, accessed
+> October 23, 2026. https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/12159030?hl=en
+
+The page gives an enforcement date but no dated announcement. For new main
+images, use the incoming minimum as your production floor. YouTube Shopping ads
+on TV already require 500 x 500 pixels. Lifestyle images have a higher
+attribute-specific minimum, below.
+
+A main image below the applicable minimum can cause product disapproval. Open
+Products, then Needs attention, and use the upcoming-enforcement warnings to
+find affected products. Check the file at the submitted URL: a small thumbnail
+can fail even when a larger master exists elsewhere. Open that URL before
+making another render.
+
+<!-- SECTION: Additional images -->
+
+## What belongs in additional_image_link?
+
+An additional image can show the reverse side. A close-up may explain a detail
+that disappears in the main view; a wider shot can show the item in use. They
+inherit the main image’s technical requirements, but Google permits staging and
+views that show only part of the product. An image of one component can also
+explain a bundle.
+
+| Check | Specification | Source |
+|---|---|---|
+| Number | Up to 10 additional images; optional | Additional image link |
+| Minimum | Before January 31, 2027: 100 x 100 px non-clothing, 250 x 250 clothing; then 500 x 500 | Additional image link; Image too small |
+| Recommended size | 1500 x 1500 px or above | Additional image link |
+| Maximum | Same as main: 64 MP and 16 MB | Additional image link; Image link |
+| Formats | JPEG, WebP, PNG, GIF, BMP, TIFF | Additional image link |
+| Background | Staging and product-in-use scenes allowed | Additional image link |
+
+> Google allows up to 10 additional images and recommends 1500 x 1500 pixels
+> or above. Method: read the attribute’s format table, notice, and exceptions
+> together, including its rule for undersized additional images.
+> Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Additional image link, undated,
+> accessed October 23, 2026.
+> https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/6324370?hl=en
+
+An additional image below the minimum won’t be shown, but it does not itself
+disapprove the product. That exception is about size, not permission to add
+promotional overlays.
+
+<!-- SECTION: Lifestyle images -->
+
+## How does lifestyle_image_link differ?
+
+This optional attribute supplies a scene for free listings: the product in use,
+staged in a room, or shown as part of a set. It is not a replacement for the
+required main image.
+
+| Check | Specification | Source |
+|---|---|---|
+| Number | Up to 5 lifestyle images | Lifestyle image link |
+| Minimum | 600 x 600 px on the attribute-specific page | Lifestyle image link |
+| Recommended size | Highest-resolution full-size image available, within the caps | Lifestyle image link |
+| Maximum | 64 MP and 16 MB | Lifestyle image link |
+| Formats | JPEG, WebP, PNG, GIF, BMP, TIFF | Lifestyle image link |
+| Background | Real-world or staged context; no borders or padding | Lifestyle image link |
+
+> The lifestyle attribute permits up to 5 images, requires at least 600 x 600
+> pixels, and gives upper limits of 64 megapixels and 16 MB. Its aspect-ratio
+> range is printed as “2:0 and 2:3”; the first value is unusable. Method:
+> direct reading of the attribute page, with that defect left uncorrected.
+> Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Lifestyle image link, undated,
+> accessed October 23, 2026.
+> https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/9103186?hl=en
+
+Google’s general Image best practices page applies primary-image resolution
+guidance to lifestyle images. The attribute page still requires 600 x 600.
+Use the higher minimum. The malformed ratio has no verified correction;
+check the intended crop in Merchant Center before preparing the full set.
+
+Source for the general guidance: Google Merchant Center Help, Image best
+practices, undated, accessed October 23, 2026.
+https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/18353357?hl=en
+
+<!-- SECTION: Disapprovals -->
+
+## What gets a Merchant Center image rejected?
+
+Read the issue named in Needs attention before changing the artwork. Google may
+simply be unable to fetch the file.
+
+| Problem | What to change | Google Help source |
+|---|---|---|
+| Added sale text, shipping claims, or a watermark | Supply a product image without the promotional layer | Text on image |
+| A border, placeholder, or unrelated item in the main image | Show the actual item sold; keep unrelated props out of the main view | Image link |
+| Wrong color or pattern | Match the pictured variant to the product and landing page | Clothing and accessories |
+| Broken or blocked URL | Serve the actual supported image file at a public, crawlable URL | Product image status |
+| File extension and format disagree | Fix the export and URL so they identify the same format | Product image status |
+
+Branding that is part of the physical product differs from a logo added over
+the photograph. Google permits the former. Its rules also contain specific
+generic-image exceptions for hardware, vehicles and parts, and software; a
+placeholder is not automatically acceptable for other categories. A set sold
+together can appear together; unrelated products are the problem in a main
+image. AI disclosure labels have a separate exception, explained below.
+
+Sources: Google Merchant Center Help, Text on image and Image link, undated,
+accessed October 23, 2026.
+https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/12158684?hl=en
+https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/6324350?hl=en
+
+For URL failures, test the exact submitted address outside a signed-in session.
+Confirm that Googlebot and Googlebot-Image can fetch it. Fixing the picture
+won’t repair an inaccessible server path.
+
+Source: Google Merchant Center Help, How to check and manage your product
+image status, undated, accessed October 23, 2026.
+https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/18353079?hl=en
+
+<!-- SECTION: Framing and variants -->
+
+## Do backgrounds, apparel, and variants need separate treatment?
+
+A white background is recommended, not universally mandatory. Google’s Image
+best practices page accepts staged images that clearly show the item. Its
+clothing guide recommends showing clothing on a model, while shoes, bags, and
+accessories appear alone in main images and on a model in additional views.
+
+For a full-body clothing photo, keep the head and feet in frame.
+
+> Google recommends a product filling 75 to 90 percent of the frame. This is
+> framing guidance, not a published width-versus-area measurement formula.
+> Method: read the recommendation in the Image best practices page.
+> Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Image best practices, undated,
+> accessed October 23, 2026.
+> https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/18353357?hl=en
+
+The clothing guide says both main and additional images
+should show the variant being sold, with the correct option selected on the
+destination page. Name the export for that variant and check it against the
+selected option, especially when similar finishes share a folder.
+
+Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Best practices for advertising clothing
+and accessories, undated, accessed October 23, 2026.
+https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/7348545?hl=en
+
+Use the white background packshot guide for production. The Platform specs hub,
+Amazon product image requirements, and Shopify product image sizes cover other
+destinations. The Shopify platform page explains the store workflow; its image
+settings do not replace Merchant Center’s feed rules.
+
+<!-- SECTION: AI metadata -->
+
+## What metadata must AI-generated product images retain?
+
+The next check is in the file, not the visible picture.
+
+Google allows AI-generated imagery subject to its image rules and requires
+metadata identifying that origin. Preserve the embedded IPTC DigitalSourceType
+property through export and delivery.
+
+> “Don’t remove embedded metadata tags” is Google’s instruction for images
+> created with generative AI. Method: direct reading of the additional-image
+> attribute’s metadata rule, also present on the main and lifestyle pages.
+> Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Additional image link, undated,
+> accessed October 23, 2026.
+> https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/6324370?hl=en
+
+IPTC’s identifier `trainedAlgorithmicMedia` describes content created with a
+trained generative model. `compositeSynthetic` describes a composite with
+generative elements. A photographed product in an AI-made setting fits that
+definition; this is an application of the vocabulary, not a separate Google
+exemption for backgrounds.
+`algorithmicMedia` covers a different process: algorithmic creation without a
+model trained on sampled content. Use the value that describes how the image
+was made.
+
+Source: IPTC NewsCodes, Digital Source Type vocabulary, checked October 23,
+2026. https://cv.iptc.org/newscodes/digitalsourcetype/trainedAlgorithmicMedia
+https://cv.iptc.org/newscodes/digitalsourcetype/compositeSynthetic
+https://cv.iptc.org/newscodes/digitalsourcetype/algorithmicMedia
+
+The Image studio supports output up to 4K, depending on the engine. Its
+transparent-background option is limited to the ChatGPT Image 2.5 engines with
+PNG or WebP. The free Image editor can crop the result. These are production
+tools, not a Merchant Center connection.
+
+> hubStudio’s help center documents output up to 4K and limits transparent
+> output to its ChatGPT Image 2.5 engines in PNG or WebP. Method: checked
+> against the current Image studio help and the binding product description.
+> Source: hubStudio Help, Create an image, checked October 23, 2026.
+> https://www.hubstudio.ai/help/create-an-image
+
+Choose Download image for the original render.
+
+Do not use Download clean copy or an Image anonymizer export for a feed: they
+strip the embedded markers. After editing, inspect the file itself. A crop or
+format conversion may leave you with different metadata, and downloading an
+original does not prove that every required tag is present.
+
+If tags are missing, correct them before submission and inspect the file
+served at the final image URL. The eCommerce design service covers work made
+with the studio team inside the app.
+
+Source: hubStudio Help, Create an image and Assets Library and the tools,
+checked October 23, 2026. https://www.hubstudio.ai/help/assets-library
+
+<!-- SECTION: Automatic improvements -->
+
+## Will automatic image improvements fix a disapproval?
+
+They may fix an overlay. Google says automatic image improvements are off by
+default; enable them under Products, Automations. Merchant Center then tries to
+remove detected text, watermarks, or logos. Successful changes can replace the
+image and restore approval. Inspect the result in Needs attention, where
+affected products show the original and improved images.
+
+Google also exempts AI disclosure labels from its overlay and watermark
+prohibitions. Do not treat that exception as permission to add a sale badge, or
+as a substitute for the embedded metadata rule. This is production practice,
+not legal advice.
+
+Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Allow Merchant Center to improve your
+product images, undated, accessed October 23, 2026.
+https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/12724659?hl=en
+
+<!-- SECTION: FAQ -->
+
+## FAQ
+
+### What size should Google Shopping images be?
+
+Use Google’s recommendation of around 1500 x 1500 pixels or above as the
+starting point for main and additional images. Check both pixel count and file
+weight before delivery. The minimum is a separate question: the table above
+distinguishes the temporary floors, the incoming general floor, and the
+lifestyle-specific requirement.
+
+### Why was my Google Merchant Center image disapproved?
+
+Read the issue in Products, Needs attention. It may concern promotional
+overlays, an undersized image, the wrong product, or a file Google cannot
+reach. Test the submitted URL before commissioning another image. If the
+problem is an overlay, replace the image or review the result of automatic
+image improvements.
+
+### Can I use AI-generated images in Google Shopping?
+
+Yes, if they meet the image rules and contain metadata identifying their AI
+origin. Preserve the embedded DigitalSourceType property, and inspect the
+delivered file after editing or conversion. Also compare the visible product
+with the actual item: a correctly tagged image can still depict the wrong
+color, shape, or variant.
+
+### What is the minimum image size for Google Merchant Center in 2027?
+
+The general minimum becomes 500 x 500 pixels on January 31, 2027. Prepare
+replacement main images before that date. Do not apply that number to every
+attribute without checking: the lifestyle page specifies a higher floor, and TV
+Shopping ads already have their own requirement. The dated table above keeps
+those cases separate.
+
+### Do Google Shopping images need a white background?
+
+Not universally. Google recommends solid white or light-neutral backgrounds for
+main images and also accepts staged images that clearly show the product.
+Lifestyle images serve a different purpose: context or use. Keep that
+distinction when preparing the set, and don’t add promotional text simply
+because an image has a lifestyle setting.
+
+### What is a lifestyle image in Merchant Center?
+
+It shows the product in a setting or in use and is submitted through the
+optional lifestyle_image_link attribute for free listings. It does not replace
+the main image. The attribute’s own page sets a higher minimum resolution than
+the general incoming rule and prohibits borders, padding, promotional elements,
+and other text.
+

+## Do not publish
+
+- A made-up announcement date. Only enforcement and warning dates are verified.
+- An inferred lifestyle ratio replacing the malformed value. Print the source
+  problem and advise checking the intended crop in Merchant Center.
+- A claim that 500 x 500 overrides the lifestyle-specific 600 x 600 row.
+- A blanket ban on every image containing multiple objects. Bundle content and
+  additional/lifestyle context have different rules.
+- A promise of approval, feed submission or automatic metadata restoration by
+  hubStudio; none is documented. Never recommend a clean-copy export for feeds.
+- Performance percentages, a claim that larger images improve conversions by a
+  stated amount, or a universal approval/review turnaround.
+- Apparel aspect-ratio and alternative resolution recommendations are outside
+  this article's size table; do not confuse them with current mandatory minima.
+- Generic-image category IDs are unnecessary. Describe exceptions without them.

# Translating hubstudio.ai into French and Chinese

Every English page of this site ships in French (`/fr/<native slug>`) and
Simplified Chinese (`/zh/<English path>`). This guide is binding for every
change that adds or edits an English page: an editorial publish run, a help
sync, a changelog sync, a page built by hand. Nothing goes live in English
only.

The glossaries next to this file, `glossary/fr.md` and `glossary/zh.md`, hold
the terms already settled in the shared dictionary. Read the one for your
language before translating anything.

## How the site is translated

- The English `.astro` pages are the only page sources. A French or Chinese
  page is the English page rendered, then rewritten by the middleware from a
  dictionary keyed by the English text (`src/i18n/core.ts`).
- Dictionaries: `src/i18n/dict/<fr|zh>/pages/<page-id>.json` per page
  (`home`, `pricing`, `resources/insights/<slug>`...), `common.json` for a
  sentence found on three pages or more (header, footer, menus, shared
  blocks), and the hand-written `js.json` (strings the client scripts ask for)
  and `server.json` (API answers).
- `src/i18n/routes.ts` gives every English page its French address. A page
  missing there has no French or Chinese version at all.
- Opt a subtree out with `data-no-i18n` (a name, a code, a quoted English
  source). Use it sparingly: it is never a way to skip a translation.

## The steps, for every new or changed page

Run from the repository root.

1. **French address.** Add the page to `src/i18n/routes.ts`: an insight to
   `ARTICLES`, a how-to to `HOWTOS`, a help article to `HELP`, a design
   service to `DESIGN`, a platform page to `PLATFORMS`, anything else to
   `FR_PATHS` directly; case studies and team pages keep their slug (`WORK`,
   `TEAM`). Keep each map in alphabetical order. The slug is native French,
   written the way a French editor would title the page, not a word-for-word
   rendering of the English slug: lowercase, words joined by hyphens, accents
   stripped (Ã© to e, Ã§ to c, Å“ to oe), apostrophes become hyphens
   (`l-erreur-d-adobe-sur-l-ia`), sixty characters at most. Brand and platform
   names stay as they are (`douyin-specifications-video-...`). **A French slug
   never changes once it is live**; if one ever must, add a 301 from the old
   address in `vercel.json` in the same commit.
2. **Extract.** `npm run i18n:local -- extract --context .i18n-work/ctx`
   It reads every English page from a dev server of this checkout (started by
   the command when none runs, stopped at the end), signs the gate cookies so
   the password-gated pages are read signed in as well, adds every new
   sentence to the dictionaries as an empty entry, drops the sentences gone
   from the pages, and writes the translator's context (reading order, tags)
   to `.i18n-work/` (ignored by git). Always extract every page, not `--only`:
   a new article also shows on the home page, the insights index and the
   insights layers, and those pages get new cards to translate too. Give the
   command up to ten minutes. If it reports that the dev server started before
   the last `.env` change, run it again with `--restart`. In Git Bash, prefix
   any command that passes a path (`--only /about`) with `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1`.
3. **See what is left.** `npm run i18n:tx -- pending fr` and
   `npm run i18n:tx -- pending zh` list every dictionary with an empty entry.
4. **Translate every pending dictionary** with the three passes below, one
   language at a time per translator. French and Chinese may run in parallel
   (two subagents), each touching only its own language.
5. **Check.** `npm run i18n:local -- check` must print
   `âœ“ every page is translated in French and Chinese`, and
   `npm run i18n:guard` must print its âœ“ line. The guard also runs before
   every build: it fails on an English page without a French address, a
   non-native slug, an empty dictionary entry or a missing localized capture.
6. **Screenshots** (see below) when the page shows the app.
7. **One commit** holds the English page and everything its translation
   touched: `src/i18n/routes.ts`, `src/i18n/dict/`, any `.fr`/`.zh` capture and
   `src/i18n/localized-images.json`.

## If the translation cannot be finished

The change does not ship. A run that cannot extract (no dev server), cannot
translate, or cannot get `check` to pass stops before the commit and says why
in its log: an editorial row stays at `image_ready` and its email reports the
failure. Never commit an English page whose French and Chinese are not done,
never paste the English into a dictionary to make the check pass, never leave
a placeholder or a marker in a dictionary. The no-TODO rule
(`editorial/CLAUDE.md`, "No TODO leaves a run") applies to translations.

Settled 2026-10-18: `/pricing/calculator` and its settings page print the live
exchange rate (an add-on price such as `$41`, the rate source or
`Unavailable`). When the rate fetch fails during an extract, those sentences
change and come back empty; that is not translation work. Restore the
committed entries (`git show HEAD:<dictionary>`) and extract again once the
rate loads, so the dictionaries keep the live-rate sentences.

Pass files left in `.i18n-work/passes/<locale>/<id>/` by an earlier run are
merged by `build` with the new ones (pass3 wins), and their indexes point at
whatever the page holds today. Delete a page's old pass files before writing
new ones.

## The three passes

The method is the `/deep-translate` skill
(`~/.claude/skills/deep-translate/SKILL.md`, with `HUMANIZER.md` for the
AI-writing tells to strip). In an unattended run its "show and pause" steps
are replaced by the pass files and `changes.md` described here.

Target: a native business journalist wrote the page from scratch. French at
the level of Les Echos or Le Monde Ã‰conomie, Chinese at the level of è´¢ç»,
36æ°ª or æ™šç‚¹ LatePost. Written register, never spoken, never chatty, never
"translated".

For each pending dictionary (`<id>` as printed by `pending`):

1. `npm run i18n:tx -- show <id> <fr|zh>` prints the units still empty,
   numbered in reading order with their tag (`h1`, `p`, `li`, `a`, `button`,
   `title`, `meta`, `json-ld`...) and attribute (`alt` is an image
   description, `aria-label` a screen-reader label, `content` an SEO meta,
   `data-*` text a script shows). Run it without the locale to read the whole
   page first: translate the meaning in context, never unit by unit. For the
   shared dictionary the id is `common` and the locale is required.
2. Write the passes into `.i18n-work/passes/<fr|zh>/<id>/` as
   `{"<index>": "<translation>"}`, values only, never the English keys:
   - `pass1.json`: Step 1, a full native rewrite of every listed unit from
     scratch (re-author; use the English only for what to say). A long page
     may be split: `pass1-a.json`, `pass1-b.json`...
   - `pass2.json`: Step 2, worked from pass 1 alone, without looking at the
     English: restructure, stronger native verbs and idioms, rhythm, no
     English-shaped clauses or noun chains. Only the units it changes.
   - `pass3.json`: Step 3, the native editor's finish on pass 2: hunt every
     last trace of translation, stiff transitions, flat phrasing. Only the
     units it changes.
   - `changes.md`: 10 to 40 lines of the main before/after across the passes,
     by section (`[section] pass1 -> pass3: ... / why: ...`).
   Do the passes for real: on a page written in one go, Steps 2 and 3
   normally change a large share of the units.
3. `npm run i18n:tx -- build <fr|zh> <id>` merges the passes (pass1 < pass2 <
   pass3) into the dictionary, leaving every other entry as it is, and checks
/**
 * The translator's bench for the three-pass method (src/i18n/TRANSLATING.md).
 *
 *   npm run i18n:tx -- pending <fr|zh>
 *       every dictionary that still holds an empty entry, with the count
 *   npm run i18n:tx -- show <page-id> [fr|zh]
 *       the page's own units (shared ones left out), numbered in reading
 *       order with their tag; with a locale, only the units still empty in it
 *   npm run i18n:tx -- build <fr|zh> <page-id>
 *       merge the pass files into the dictionary, then check the whole file
 *       against the house rules (scripts/i18n-rules.mjs); exit 1 on a
 *       problem or an entry still empty
 *
 * page-id: the dictionary's name under src/i18n/dict/<locale>/pages/
 * (home, pricing, resources/insights/<slug>...), or `common` for the shared
 * dictionary (show and build then need the locale; its units are numbered in
 * the order of that locale's common.json).
 *
 * Reading order and tags come from the context files written by
 *   npm run i18n:local -- extract --context .i18n-work/ctx
 * Run that first, and again after any change to an English page.
 *
 * Pass files, in .i18n-work/passes/<locale>/<page-id>/ :
 *   pass1*.json  {"<index>": "<translation>"}  Step 1, every index to translate
 *                (a long page may be split: pass1-a.json, pass1-b.json...)
 *   pass2.json   only the indexes Step 2 changed
 *   pass3.json   only the indexes Step 3 changed
 *   changes.md   10 to 40 lines: the main before/after across the passes
 * Later passes win (pass1 < pass2 < pass3). build writes only the indexes
 * found in the pass files: every other translation in the dictionary stays
 * as it is, so a changed page never loses its edited sentences.
 *
 * .i18n-work/ is ignored by git. Same file in the other site's repository
 * (hubstudio / BearingBridgeCOM): keep the two in step.
 */
import { existsSync, mkdirSync, readFileSync, readdirSync, writeFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { dirname, join, relative, resolve } from 'node:path';
import { problems } from './i18n-rules.mjs';

const root = resolve(import.meta.dirname, '..');
const DICT = join(root, 'src', 'i18n', 'dict');
const WORK = join(root, '.i18n-work');
const CTX = join(WORK, 'ctx');
const LOCALES = ['fr', 'zh'];

const readJson = (f) => (existsSync(f) ? JSON.parse(readFileSync(f, 'utf8')) : {});
const writeJson = (f, data) => {
  mkdirSync(dirname(f), { recursive: true });
  writeFileSync(f, JSON.stringify(data, null, 2) + '\n');
};
const walk = (d) =>
  existsSync(d)
    ? readdirSync(d, { withFileTypes: true }).flatMap((e) => (e.isDirectory() ? walk(join(d, e.name)) : [join(d, e.name)]))
    : [];
const rel = (f) => relative(root, f).replace(/\\/g, '/');
const idOf = (base, file) => relative(base, file).replace(/\\/g, '/').replace(/\.json$/, '');
const dictFile = (locale, id) => (id === 'common' ? join(DICT, locale, 'common.json') : join(DICT, locale, 'pages', `${id}.json`));
const fail = (msg) => {
  console.error(`âœ— ${msg}`);
  process.exit(2);
};
const needLocale = (l) => {
  if (!LOCALES.includes(l)) fail(`locale must be ${LOCALES.join(' or ')}`);
};

/** Tag and page of every key, from the context files. */
function keyInfo() {
  const info = new Map();
  for (const f of walk(CTX)) {
    const ctx = readJson(f);
    for (const u of ctx.units ?? []) if (!info.has(u.key)) info.set(u.key, { tag: u.tag, attr: u.attr, path: ctx.path });
  }
  return info;
}

/** The units a dictionary is built from, in order: [{key, tag, attr}]. */
function unitsOf(locale, id) {
  if (id === 'common') {
    const info = keyInfo();
    return Object.keys(readJson(dictFile(locale, 'common'))).map((key) => ({ key, ...(info.get(key) ?? { tag: '?' }) }));
  }
  const file = join(CTX, `${id}.json`);
  if (!existsSync(file)) fail(`no context for ${id}: run  npm run i18n:local -- extract --context .i18n-work/ctx`);
  return readJson(file).units.filter((u) => !u.common);
}

const [cmd, a, b] = process.argv.slice(2);

if (cmd === 'pending') {
  needLocale(a);
  let total = 0;
  const rows = [];
  for (const f of walk(join(DICT, a))) {
    const empty = Object.values(readJson(f)).filter((v) => !v).length;
    if (!empty) continue;
    const name = idOf(join(DICT, a), f);
    const id = name.startsWith('pages/') ? name.slice(6) : name;
    const handBuilt = id === 'js' || id === 'server';
    rows.push(`${id}: ${empty} empty${handBuilt ? ' (hand-written dictionary: fill it in the JSON file itself)' : ''}`);
    total += empty;

+---
+title: Google Merchant Center Image Requirements 2026
+slug: google-merchant-center-image-requirements
+description: Google Shopping image rules per attribute: sizes, file caps, formats, what gets disapproved, the 500 px minimum from January 2027 and the AI image rule.
+excerpt: Match each product image to its feed attribute, prepare for the new minimum size, and keep AI metadata through the final export for Merchant Center.
+template: spec
+---
+
+<!-- HERO SECTION -->
+
+# Google Shopping image requirements for 2026
+
+Reviewed October 23, 2026. By Cyril Drouin.
+
+Merchant Center checks the picture and the file behind its URL. The image
+attribute determines which rules apply. Today’s minimum and the coming minimum
+are different, and AI metadata must survive the export.
+
+<!-- INTRODUCTION -->
+
+## What are the Google Shopping image requirements?
+
+Google Shopping image requirements cover the pictured product, file size, and
+crawlable URL. Prepare main images at Google’s recommended 1500 x 1500 pixels
+or above, keep AI metadata, and check the dated minimums below. Lifestyle
+images have their own rules. hubStudio supplies image creation and export; you
+submit the URLs through your Merchant Center data source.
+
+### Main image: image_link
+
+| Check | Specification | Source |
+|---|---|---|
+| Required image | Main view of the item being sold | Image link |
+| Before January 31, 2027 | 100 x 100 px non-clothing; 250 x 250 px clothing | Image too small |
+| TV Shopping ads now | 500 x 500 px minimum | Image too small |
+| From January 31, 2027 | 500 x 500 px for all products | Image too small |
+| Recommended size | Around 1500 x 1500 px or above | Image link |
+| Maximum | 64 megapixels; 16 MB | Image link |
+| Formats | JPEG, WebP, PNG, GIF, BMP, TIFF | Image link |
+| Background | Solid white or light neutral recommended; clear staged images also acceptable | Image best practices |
+
+> Google recommends around 1500 x 1500 pixels or above for the main image.
+> Its attribute table lists a ceiling of 64 megapixels and 16 MB. Method:
+> direct reading of the published formatting specifications.
+> Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Image link, undated, accessed October
+> 23, 2026. https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/6324350?hl=en
+
+Keep exports below both ceilings. The Image too big help page says “less
+than” in its headline and “cannot be larger than” in its body. Avoid that
+boundary when exporting.
+
+Measure file weight and pixel count separately.
+
+Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Image too big, undated, accessed October
+23, 2026. https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/12473903?hl=en
+
+<!-- SECTION: Minimum-size transition -->
+
+## When does the new minimum image size apply?
+
+Google’s attribute table already prints the incoming minimum. Its dedicated
+Image too small page explains the transition:
+
+> “Enforcement of the new requirements will begin January 31, 2027.” The new
+> general minimum is 500 x 500 pixels. Until then, the stated floors remain
+> 100 x 100 for non-clothing and 250 x 250 for clothing. Warnings began in
+> July 2026. Method: read the dated transition notice alongside the temporary
+> requirements on the same page.
+> Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Image too small, undated, accessed
+> October 23, 2026. https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/12159030?hl=en
+
+The page gives an enforcement date but no dated announcement. For new main
+images, use the incoming minimum as your production floor. YouTube Shopping ads
+on TV already require 500 x 500 pixels. Lifestyle images have a higher
+attribute-specific minimum, below.
+
+A main image below the applicable minimum can cause product disapproval. Open
+Products, then Needs attention, and use the upcoming-enforcement warnings to
+find affected products. Check the file at the submitted URL: a small thumbnail
+can fail even when a larger master exists elsewhere. Open that URL before
+making another render.
+
+<!-- SECTION: Additional images -->
+
+## What belongs in additional_image_link?
+
+An additional image can show the reverse side. A close-up may explain a detail
+that disappears in the main view; a wider shot can show the item in use. They
+inherit the main image’s technical requirements, but Google permits staging and
+views that show only part of the product. An image of one component can also
+explain a bundle.
+
+| Check | Specification | Source |
+|---|---|---|
+| Number | Up to 10 additional images; optional | Additional image link |
+| Minimum | Before January 31, 2027: 100 x 100 px non-clothing, 250 x 250 clothing; then 500 x 500 | Additional image link; Image too small |
+| Recommended size | 1500 x 1500 px or above | Additional image link |
+| Maximum | Same as main: 64 MP and 16 MB | Additional image link; Image link |
+| Formats | JPEG, WebP, PNG, GIF, BMP, TIFF | Additional image link |
+| Background | Staging and product-in-use scenes allowed | Additional image link |
+
+> Google allows up to 10 additional images and recommends 1500 x 1500 pixels
+> or above. Method: read the attribute’s format table, notice, and exceptions
+> together, including its rule for undersized additional images.
+> Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Additional image link, undated,
+> accessed October 23, 2026.
+> https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/6324370?hl=en
+
+An additional image below the minimum won’t be shown, but it does not itself
+disapprove the product. That exception is about size, not permission to add
+promotional overlays.
+
+<!-- SECTION: Lifestyle images -->
+
+## How does lifestyle_image_link differ?
+
+This optional attribute supplies a scene for free listings: the product in use,
+staged in a room, or shown as part of a set. It is not a replacement for the
+required main image.
+
+| Check | Specification | Source |
+|---|---|---|
+| Number | Up to 5 lifestyle images | Lifestyle image link |
+| Minimum | 600 x 600 px on the attribute-specific page | Lifestyle image link |
+| Recommended size | Highest-resolution full-size image available, within the caps | Lifestyle image link |
+| Maximum | 64 MP and 16 MB | Lifestyle image link |
+| Formats | JPEG, WebP, PNG, GIF, BMP, TIFF | Lifestyle image link |
+| Background | Real-world or staged context; no borders or padding | Lifestyle image link |
+
+> The lifestyle attribute permits up to 5 images, requires at least 600 x 600
+> pixels, and gives upper limits of 64 megapixels and 16 MB. Its aspect-ratio
+> range is printed as “2:0 and 2:3”; the first value is unusable. Method:
+> direct reading of the attribute page, with that defect left uncorrected.
+> Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Lifestyle image link, undated,
+> accessed October 23, 2026.
+> https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/9103186?hl=en
+
+Google’s general Image best practices page applies primary-image resolution
+guidance to lifestyle images. The attribute page still requires 600 x 600.
+Use the higher minimum. The malformed ratio has no verified correction;
+check the intended crop in Merchant Center before preparing the full set.
+
+Source for the general guidance: Google Merchant Center Help, Image best
+practices, undated, accessed October 23, 2026.
+https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/18353357?hl=en
+
+<!-- SECTION: Disapprovals -->
+
+## What gets a Merchant Center image rejected?
+
+Read the issue named in Needs attention before changing the artwork. Google may
+simply be unable to fetch the file.
+
+| Problem | What to change | Google Help source |
+|---|---|---|
+| Added sale text, shipping claims, or a watermark | Supply a product image without the promotional layer | Text on image |
+| A border, placeholder, or unrelated item in the main image | Show the actual item sold; keep unrelated props out of the main view | Image link |
+| Wrong color or pattern | Match the pictured variant to the product and landing page | Clothing and accessories |
+| Broken or blocked URL | Serve the actual supported image file at a public, crawlable URL | Product image status |
+| File extension and format disagree | Fix the export and URL so they identify the same format | Product image status |
+
+Branding that is part of the physical product differs from a logo added over
+the photograph. Google permits the former. Its rules also contain specific
+generic-image exceptions for hardware, vehicles and parts, and software; a
+placeholder is not automatically acceptable for other categories. A set sold
+together can appear together; unrelated products are the problem in a main
+image. AI disclosure labels have a separate exception, explained below.
+
+Sources: Google Merchant Center Help, Text on image and Image link, undated,
+accessed October 23, 2026.
+https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/12158684?hl=en
+https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/6324350?hl=en
+
+For URL failures, test the exact submitted address outside a signed-in session.
+Confirm that Googlebot and Googlebot-Image can fetch it. Fixing the picture
+won’t repair an inaccessible server path.
+
+Source: Google Merchant Center Help, How to check and manage your product
+image status, undated, accessed October 23, 2026.
+https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/18353079?hl=en
+
+<!-- SECTION: Framing and variants -->
+
+## Do backgrounds, apparel, and variants need separate treatment?
+
+A white background is recommended, not universally mandatory. Google’s Image
+best practices page accepts staged images that clearly show the item. Its
+clothing guide recommends showing clothing on a model, while shoes, bags, and
+accessories appear alone in main images and on a model in additional views.
+
+For a full-body clothing photo, keep the head and feet in frame.
+
+> Google recommends a product filling 75 to 90 percent of the frame. This is
+> framing guidance, not a published width-versus-area measurement formula.
+> Method: read the recommendation in the Image best practices page.
+> Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Image best practices, undated,
+> accessed October 23, 2026.
+> https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/18353357?hl=en
+
+The clothing guide says both main and additional images
+should show the variant being sold, with the correct option selected on the
+destination page. Name the export for that variant and check it against the
+selected option, especially when similar finishes share a folder.
+
+Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Best practices for advertising clothing
+and accessories, undated, accessed October 23, 2026.
+https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/7348545?hl=en
+
+Use the white background packshot guide for production. The Platform specs hub,
+Amazon product image requirements, and Shopify product image sizes cover other
+destinations. The Shopify platform page explains the store workflow; its image
+settings do not replace Merchant Center’s feed rules.
+
+<!-- SECTION: AI metadata -->
+
+## What metadata must AI-generated product images retain?
+
+The next check is in the file, not the visible picture.
+
+Google allows AI-generated imagery subject to its image rules and requires
+metadata identifying that origin. Preserve the embedded IPTC DigitalSourceType
+property through export and delivery.
+
+> “Don’t remove embedded metadata tags” is Google’s instruction for images
+> created with generative AI. Method: direct reading of the additional-image
+> attribute’s metadata rule, also present on the main and lifestyle pages.
+> Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Additional image link, undated,
+> accessed October 23, 2026.
+> https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/6324370?hl=en
+
+IPTC’s identifier `trainedAlgorithmicMedia` describes content created with a
+trained generative model. `compositeSynthetic` describes a composite with
+generative elements. A photographed product in an AI-made setting fits that
+definition; this is an application of the vocabulary, not a separate Google
+exemption for backgrounds.
+`algorithmicMedia` covers a different process: algorithmic creation without a
+model trained on sampled content. Use the value that describes how the image
+was made.
+
+Source: IPTC NewsCodes, Digital Source Type vocabulary, checked October 23,
+2026. https://cv.iptc.org/newscodes/digitalsourcetype/trainedAlgorithmicMedia
+https://cv.iptc.org/newscodes/digitalsourcetype/compositeSynthetic
+https://cv.iptc.org/newscodes/digitalsourcetype/algorithmicMedia
+
+The Image studio supports output up to 4K, depending on the engine. Its
+transparent-background option is limited to the ChatGPT Image 2.5 engines with
+PNG or WebP. The free Image editor can crop the result. These are production
+tools, not a Merchant Center connection.
+
+> hubStudio’s help center documents output up to 4K and limits transparent
+> output to its ChatGPT Image 2.5 engines in PNG or WebP. Method: checked
+> against the current Image studio help and the binding product description.
+> Source: hubStudio Help, Create an image, checked October 23, 2026.
+> https://www.hubstudio.ai/help/create-an-image
+
+Choose Download image for the original render.
+
+Do not use Download clean copy or an Image anonymizer export for a feed: they
+strip the embedded markers. After editing, inspect the file itself. A crop or
+format conversion may leave you with different metadata, and downloading an
+original does not prove that every required tag is present.
+
+If tags are missing, correct them before submission and inspect the file
+served at the final image URL. The eCommerce design service covers work made
+with the studio team inside the app.
+
+Source: hubStudio Help, Create an image and Assets Library and the tools,
+checked October 23, 2026. https://www.hubstudio.ai/help/assets-library
+
+<!-- SECTION: Automatic improvements -->
+
+## Will automatic image improvements fix a disapproval?
+
+They may fix an overlay. Google says automatic image improvements are off by
+default; enable them under Products, Automations. Merchant Center then tries to
+remove detected text, watermarks, or logos. Successful changes can replace the
+image and restore approval. Inspect the result in Needs attention, where
+affected products show the original and improved images.
+
+Google also exempts AI disclosure labels from its overlay and watermark
+prohibitions. Do not treat that exception as permission to add a sale badge, or
+as a substitute for the embedded metadata rule. This is production practice,
+not legal advice.
+
+Source: Google Merchant Center Help, Allow Merchant Center to improve your
+product images, undated, accessed October 23, 2026.
+https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/12724659?hl=en
+
+<!-- SECTION: FAQ -->
+
+## FAQ
+
+### What size should Google Shopping images be?
+
+Use Google’s recommendation of around 1500 x 1500 pixels or above as the
+starting point for main and additional images. Check both pixel count and file
+weight before delivery. The minimum is a separate question: the table above
+distinguishes the temporary floors, the incoming general floor, and the
+lifestyle-specific requirement.
+
+### Why was my Google Merchant Center image disapproved?
+
+Read the issue in Products, Needs attention. It may concern promotional
+overlays, an undersized image, the wrong product, or a file Google cannot
+reach. Test the submitted URL before commissioning another image. If the
+problem is an overlay, replace the image or review the result of automatic
+image improvements.
+
+### Can I use AI-generated images in Google Shopping?
+
+Yes, if they meet the image rules and contain metadata identifying their AI
+origin. Preserve the embedded DigitalSourceType property, and inspect the
+delivered file after editing or conversion. Also compare the visible product
+with the actual item: a correctly tagged image can still depict the wrong
+color, shape, or variant.
+
+### What is the minimum image size for Google Merchant Center in 2027?
+
+The general minimum becomes 500 x 500 pixels on January 31, 2027. Prepare
+replacement main images before that date. Do not apply that number to every
+attribute without checking: the lifestyle page specifies a higher floor, and TV
+Shopping ads already have their own requirement. The dated table above keeps
+those cases separate.
+
+### Do Google Shopping images need a white background?
+
+Not universally. Google recommends solid white or light-neutral backgrounds for
+main images and also accepts staged images that clearly show the product.
+Lifestyle images serve a different purpose: context or use. Keep that
+distinction when preparing the set, and don’t add promotional text simply
+because an image has a lifestyle setting.
+
+### What is a lifestyle image in Merchant Center?
+
+It shows the product in a setting or in use and is submitted through the
+optional lifestyle_image_link attribute for free listings. It does not replace
+the main image. The attribute’s own page sets a higher minimum resolution than
+the general incoming rule and prohibits borders, padding, promotional elements,
+and other text.
+
